title: South America 1960: Caracas, Rio and Buenos Aires musicians
summary: Touring South America with a 20-piece book, Lee found the Buenos Aires players excellent, Rio's strings great and horns terrible.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: So we did that thing, and then we went to South America in 1960, and that was an experience that I think musicians should have because -- they say music is an international language, and it is -- and that's when you find out that it is. Because our first stop was in Caracas, Venezuela, and from Caracaus we went to Rio. Now, the difference is just amazing, the way the music is. In Caracas, you find they are really heavy in to the rhythms, you know, and the musicians are fair; you know, I'm speaking of the string players, fair, horn players, are fair -- you get to Rio; string players are great; rhythm is good, horn players are horrible, you know; just terrible. Then you go to Argentina -- we had the most pleasant surprise of our lives in Buenos Aires, when I put the music up in front of these guys and they started playing this music, you thought it was Basie, you thought it was Woodie, you thought it was any good band back in the states -- any of them. They could play! They were different; they played all the instruments well.
So you traveled with a book for a large orchestra.

Oh, 18 or 20. We could -- but we had to cut the strings down, you know, because of the expense. But the book really was for 20 strings. And like, 5 woodwinds and 6 brass; we had a big book, and these guys cut that music and played so good, you know, you just knew you were home.

That's right. And incidentally, the same thing happened in Japan. But all over South America, each country you'd go to there, you'd find the caliber of musicians, some of them just don't play some instruments well -- but overall, Argentina had the best musicians of any place that we had been.
